newsitem.title: USA: S&P says Oregon's Measure 47 may weaken ratings.
newsitem.headline: S&P says Oregon's Measure 47 may weaken ratings.

text.p: Standard & Poor's Corp said on Monday it may initiate comprehensive reviews of selected Oregon municipal credits should voters approve a controversial property tax measure on the November 5 ballot.
S&P said passage of Measure 47 could have long-term negative credit implications for municipal issuers.

The measure would roll back fiscal 1998 property taxes by a pro rata 20 percent and cap future property tax growth. According to state estimates, schools and local governments would lose about $1 billion in the first two years.

In Monday's CreditWeek Municipal newsletter, S&P said the effect of Measure 47 on local ratings would depend on several factors, including the state's allocation formula, management's ability to restructure government services, and local support for tax increases above the formula.

If the state were to allocate the rollback disproportionately, so that some entities face a larger cut, those entities would be under more pressure to keep their budgets in line and maintain credit quality, S&P said.

The rating agency said the state would likely face pressure to ease the burden of property tax losses, especially for schools. Maintenance of the state's rating would depend in part on the state's management of fiscal pressures resulting from the measure, S&P said.

While bonded debt generally is exempted from the rollback and annual increase limit, the measure would have significant fiscal effects and further erode the financial flexibility of local governments in Oregon, S&P said.
The long-term risk of Measure 47 for most local governments may be credit deterioration over time as a result of reduced flexibility to finance growth, S&P said.

Measure 47's impact could be even more significant for special districts. Unlike cities and counties, special districts' revenues typically are concentrated in property taxes, the rating agency said. --Adam Entous, 415-677-2511
